text:
A: Hiya! Oh, can you hear me? I think it's working, yeah?
B: I can hear you. Yes.
A: Oh good, good. Sorry, my internet is sometimes, you know, it goes funny. I'm Sana. I'm in Bolton.
B: Abena. Croydon, Thornton Heath.
A: Ah, London! Acha. I always want to go London properly, like shopping and everything, but my husband he says it's too expensive, which is true, yeah? Did you do that puzzle thing at the start? I was so stressed, honestly. I was thinking, is this a test, like, will they think I'm stupid? I did like half of it and then the timer was finished.
B: It's not a test. It said at the beginning. I did some of it. Some of them didn't make sense, the shapes ones.
A: Yes! The shapes ones! I was turning my head like this, you know. Erm, so what do you do? Are you at work today or...?
B: I'm a senior care assistant. Care home in Norbury, older people. I finished a long day yesterday, twelve hours. Today I'm off.
A: Oh my God, twelve hours. You must be knackered. I couldn't do that, honestly. I work in a warehouse, sort of fashion, like online fashion, so I do the parcels, packing, all of that. But it's part-time, so like three, four shifts. And they keep changing my shift, it got changed again this week. I'm so tired.
B: Part-time and you are tired?
A: [laughs] I know, I know! But it's the standing, you know. And the supervisors, they're always watching your rate, how many you done. I like the girls though, we chat all the time. Too much, he says, my supervisor. [laughs]
B: Mm. In my place if the staff are chatting and on their phones, the residents are waiting. Somebody is sitting in a wet pad because the agency girl is on TikTok. So I don't have patience for it.
A: No, no, yeah, that's different, that's people, yeah? Parcels don't care. [laughs] Erm... Do you like it, the care job?
B: I'm good at it. Like is another thing. The families trust me because I tell them the truth. If their mother is going down, I tell them. Some managers don't like that. That's it.
A: That's nice though, that's honest. My mother-in-law, she says English people put their parents in homes, but I think, you know, if somebody is looking after them proper like you, it's not bad, is it?
B: Some homes are bad. Mine is okay. Also not everybody has a family to do it. Not everybody has a mother-in-law down the road.
A: Yeah, true. Mine is literally few streets away, I go every day nearly. She makes karahi, oh my God, so much better than mine. I learned from her, not my mum, my mum is in Lahore. Are you from... sorry, can I ask where you're from originally?
B: Ghana. Kumasi.
A: Oh nice! Do you go back?
B: Every two, three years. I'm saving now. The flights are crazy.
A: Same! Lahore every couple of years, I take like three suitcases, all gifts. And there's my cousin's wedding coming, I'm doing the mehndi for everybody, I do mehndi designs, like the henna. I'm doing a course as well, lashes, beauty. I want to do my own business on Instagram, like bookings, a proper room.
B: You finished the course?
A: Erm... not yet. [laughs] Nearly. Sort of halfway.
B: Finish it. Then talk about the room.
A: [laughs] You sound like my sister! Okay, okay, I will finish it, yaar.
B: I'm serious. I didn't finish my secretarial course in Ghana, one year, and then I came here and it was too late. Nobody gives you the time back.
A: Yeah... I left my BA also, when I got married. Twenty I was. Sometimes I think about it, you know.
B: So finish this one.
